headline: The first leaf in breadth-first order is nearest
statement: Return the number of nodes on the shortest root-to-leaf path of a binary tree. A leaf has no left or right child. An empty tree has depth zero. Inputs are level-order arrays with null for absent children.
prerequisites: Basic Python lists, loops, and functions
intuition: Use a queue to visit the shallowest nodes first. The first leaf you reach ends the shortest root-to-leaf path. Return its depth immediately. A node with one missing child is not a leaf, so an empty child must not be mistaken for a shorter finished path.
approach: Return zero for an absent root.
Queue (root,1), recording depth in nodes rather than edges.
Pop nodes and return depth only if both children are absent.
correctness: FIFO order processes nodes in nondecreasing depth. The first node with no children ends a valid root-to-leaf path, and no shallower leaf can remain unprocessed. Its depth is thus minimal. A missing root has no path and correctly returns zero.
bruteForce: DFS every leaf and take the smallest depth, taking O(n) time but always traversing the whole tree even when a leaf is near the root.

complexity.explanation: Each visited node is enqueued once, with at most O(w) nodes across the active frontiers. Early exit can inspect far fewer than n nodes. Here w is the maximum number of nodes on any tree level; the queue can span parts of two consecutive levels.

pitfalls: A node with one missing child is not a leaf.
Count nodes: a root leaf has depth one.
Do not take min(0,childDepth) for a one-child node in a recursive variant.
